study.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, To Timothy, my true child in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
study.setting: Who. Paul, near the end of his life, to Timothy, his closest coworker for some fifteen years (Acts 16:1–3; 2 Timothy 1:5). Where. Ephesus, chief city of Asia, home of the great temple of Artemis; Paul spent nearly three years there and warned its elders that wolves would come (Acts 19; 20:29–31). When. Most likely AD 62–64, after Paul’s release from his first Roman imprisonment. Why. “Remain at Ephesus so that you may charge certain persons not to teach any different doctrine” (1:3): a field manual for a young leader cleaning up a hard situation. Why the greeting matters. A letter to a friend that opens with credentials, read aloud to the church; every line puts Paul’s authority behind Timothy before Timothy has to use it.

words.note: One sent with the sender’s authority: an envoy, not a volunteer. From apostello, to send. Paul did not appoint himself (Galatians 1:1). Timothy’s authority in Ephesus rests on this word.
By order. A word used for royal and divine decrees. Elsewhere Paul writes “by the will of God” (2 Timothy 1:1); here he is stronger. He is under orders. Same phrase in Titus 1:3.

Rescuer, deliverer, keeper. The Old Testament title of the LORD: “besides me there is no savior” (Isaiah 43:11). In a city that hailed Caesar as savior, Paul gives the title to God. Used of the Father (2:3; 4:10) and of the Son (2 Timothy 1:10; Titus 2:13).
Confident expectation of a sure good, not wishful thinking. Here hope is a person, not a mood: “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (Colossians 1:27).

words.word: my true child in the faith
words.note: Gnesios: legitimate, genuine, born in wedlock; the real thing, not a counterfeit. Teknon: child, a word of family and affection. “In the faith” names the family: spiritual. Paul probably led him to Christ on his first visit to Lystra (Acts 14:6–7). The same root appears when Paul says no one else “will be genuinely concerned for your welfare” (Philippians 2:20).

Grace: God’s undeserved favor, the source. Mercy: his compassion toward the helpless; the Greek Old Testament often uses it for hesed, the LORD’s steadfast love. Peace: shalom, wholeness with God, the result. Paul’s letters usually say “grace and peace”; only the two letters to Timothy add mercy. Paul knows it firsthand: “I received mercy” (1:13, 16).

words.word: from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord
words.note: One “from” governs both names: Father and Son are one source of every blessing. Kyrios, Lord, is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the LORD’s name. A small phrase with a high view of Christ.

reflect: Paul answers to a command; Timothy answers to Paul. Who holds you to account this week, and what would you want them to ask you?
“By command of God.” Where this week are you acting under orders, and where only on preference?
Who was a Paul to you? Who is your Timothy now, by name, and what would “my true child” sound like from you this week, said where others can hear it?
Grace, mercy, peace, then the charge. Which of your men needs mercy from you before he needs direction?
study.prayer: Father, you are God our Savior, and Christ Jesus is our hope. Thank you for grace I did not earn, mercy that keeps me, and peace that holds. Make me a true son in the faith, and a Paul to the men in my care: present, quick to back them, faithful to hand on what I was given. Keep me under your command today, not my own. In Jesus’ name, amen.
